frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control through Sonatrach, but European buyers seek diversified supplies and greater contractual flexibility. Gas revenues remain exposed to demand shifts and external pricing pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara and Sahel pressure
frictionVectors.details: Regional rivalry with Morocco and instability across the Sahel complicate transport, security, and diplomatic alignment. These pressures reinforce Algiers's preference for strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: External control of strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor attracts major US, European, and Chinese interest because of its access to copper and cobalt supply chains. Angola gains investment and leverage, but risks becoming a transit platform for externally controlled mineral flows.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains central to fiscal stability despite diversification efforts. International operators, debt obligations, and volatile prices continue to constrain sovereign control over long-term resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Niger trade and pipeline disruption
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Niger have disrupted established trade routes and complicated the operating environment around the Niger-Benin oil export corridor. Benin is balancing economic interdependence with regional security and diplomatic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-backed infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, road, and energy expansion relies heavily on external finance and contractors, particularly from China and Western partners. This improves connectivity while limiting domestic control over strategic infrastructure terms.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation pressure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has secured stronger terms and greater downstream ambition in its diamond relationship with De Beers. However, market concentration and weak global diamond demand still limit the pace of sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals diversification
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals could reduce diamond dependence, but foreign capital and technical expertise remain necessary. The challenge is converting exploration activity into domestic processing and durable fiscal gains.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security and mining influence
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou is deepening security ties with Russia while seeking greater state control over gold production. The arrangement may reduce Western leverage but risks opaque concessions, dependency, and weak accountability.

frictionVectors.title: Artisanal mining and territorial loss
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence and informal extraction undermine state control across gold-producing regions. Revenue leakage, displaced communities, and insecure transport corridors continue to limit effective resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking foreign capital and infrastructure for its large nickel reserves, leaving bargaining power and processing capacity largely outside national control.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Friction
frictionVectors.details: Strained relations with Rwanda and instability in eastern DRC complicate border security, trade routes, and access to mineral markets.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde is leveraging its ports and location between Europe, West Africa, and the Americas, but remains dependent on external partners for maritime surveillance and logistics investment.

frictionVectors.title: Transatlantic Trafficking Routes
frictionVectors.details: Drug-trafficking networks exploit the islands' maritime position, testing limited enforcement capacity and creating pressure from European and American security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The Kribi port complex, associated rail links, and major energy projects deepen Cameroon’s trade capacity while also increasing reliance on Chinese and other foreign capital.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside instability near Nigeria and the Central African Republic, disrupts transport, agriculture, and resource administration.

frictionVectors.title: Security Concessions and Mining Access
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security structures remain central to regime protection and are associated with privileged access to gold and diamond networks, limiting transparent national oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Corridor Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on routes through Cameroon and neighboring states exposes the country to border insecurity, customs bottlenecks, and spillover from Sudan and eastern DRC conflicts.

highlights: Oil and Gold Anchor the State

frictionVectors.title: Sudan War Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Fighting in Sudan has driven refugee flows, armed-group movement, and cross-border trafficking into eastern Chad, placing pressure on national security and humanitarian infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Gold Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad’s oil exports rely on the Cameroon pipeline corridor, while gold production in the north is shaped by informal and foreign-linked networks that weaken state capture of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: French sovereignty and maritime access
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved Mayotte dispute limits Comoros's control over migration policy, maritime jurisdiction, and regional diplomacy. French security and administrative influence remains decisive around the archipelago.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and aid dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited state capacity leaves fisheries, port development, and infrastructure financing vulnerable to outside leverage, particularly from France, Gulf partners, and multilateral lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral concessions and supply-chain control
frictionVectors.details: Copper, cobalt, and other strategic minerals attract intense competition among Chinese, Western, and regional actors. Weak contract enforcement and limited domestic processing reduce Kinshasa's ability to capture value.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern armed conflict and regional intervention
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups, cross-border networks, and allegations of external support continue to constrain state authority in the east. Security dependence on regional and international partners complicates sovereign control over transport and mining corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains the core source of fiscal and export revenue, leaving Brazzaville exposed to price cycles and the bargaining power of international energy companies. Domestic refining and diversification remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-finance exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, ports, and public works expand connectivity but can increase debt and contractor dependence. The resulting infrastructure gains do not yet translate into broad domestic control of strategic logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire retains major production power but captures a limited share of downstream value, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to global pricing and multinational processing concentration.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital and strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, energy, telecommunications, and transport corridors rely heavily on foreign investors and lenders. Abidjan is improving regulatory capacity, but external capital remains important to national development and security.

frictionVectors.title: Competing foreign military presence
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities provide revenue and diplomatic leverage but make Djibouti's security posture dependent on rival external powers. Regional crises can sharply raise pressure on its balancing strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Control of logistics corridors and port infrastructure is central to national sovereignty, yet debt and concession relationships—especially involving Chinese-linked projects—limit Djibouti's room to maneuver over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing and Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: IMF conditions and major Gulf investments provide essential liquidity but narrow Cairo's room to manage strategic assets and economic policy independently.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water and GERD Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to view Ethiopia's dam operations as a core national-security risk, with negotiations producing limited guarantees on drought-year water flows.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Depletion
frictionVectors.details: Falling oil and gas output is weakening state revenue while foreign operators retain important technical and financing leverage over remaining projects.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Malabo's large infrastructure ambitions rely on external contractors and commercial partners, creating exposure to debt, maintenance, and underutilization risks.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's Red Sea position gives it bargaining power amid rival Gulf and regional security interests, but renewed tensions with Ethiopia could destabilize border and port calculations.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Sanctions Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects generate hard currency, yet dependence on foreign mining expertise and continuing rights scrutiny limit the durability of sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Trade and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South Africa for trade access, electricity, and regional logistics, leaving its economic sovereignty sensitive to Pretoria's conditions and disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-Intensive Agriculture
frictionVectors.details: Sugar and forestry remain important export pillars but expose the kingdom to climate stress, water competition, and external market standards.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Ethiopia's control over electricity and water infrastructure, while unresolved tensions with Egypt and Sudan keep the project geopolitically exposed.

frictionVectors.title: Debt Restructuring and Corridor Access
frictionVectors.details: Debt negotiations and reliance on external lenders constrain policy space, while conflict and insecurity threaten transport corridors, energy assets, and investor confidence.

highlights: Transition government consolidates control over oil and manganese
Libreville balances France, China, and new Gulf partners

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state participation and local value addition in oil, manganese, and timber. Renegotiation risks investor hesitation and disputes with established foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Post-coup external balancing
frictionVectors.details: The transition is reducing dependence on France while courting China, the United States, and Gulf capital. This diversification creates leverage but complicates security and infrastructure partnerships.

highlights: Senegal remains the essential economic corridor
Fragile state capacity limits control over fisheries and trade

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked transport dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegalese territory, roads, and regional trade networks. Border disruptions or disagreements over transit fees can quickly affect food prices and port access.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and coastal sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fishing and weak enforcement threaten local livelihoods and maritime resource control. Donor-funded surveillance has improved capacity but has not eliminated illegal or opaque extraction.

highlights: Debt stabilization opens space for resource-policy reform
Gold remains strong while cocoa and lithium face pressure

frictionVectors.title: Mining governance and illegal gold extraction
frictionVectors.details: The state is trying to formalize artisanal mining and retain more value from gold while curbing environmental damage. Foreign-linked trading networks and local political protection continue to undermine enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is attracting interest in lithium, bauxite, and manganese processing, but financing and infrastructure constraints limit bargaining power. Accra faces pressure to choose between rapid investment and stronger domestic beneficiation rules.

highlights: Junta-led resource nationalism meets infrastructure dependence

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor control
frictionVectors.details: The rail, port, and mining complex is expanding Guinea's strategic importance while tying the country to major foreign investors and contractors. Disputes over ownership, revenue transparency, and local content remain acute.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Guinea's economy remains heavily dependent on foreign-operated bauxite exports, particularly Chinese-linked supply chains. The transition authorities seek greater state control but lack the financing and technical capacity to replace external operators.

highlights: Cashew dependence leaves the economy externally exposed
Political instability weakens control of ports and borders

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak port infrastructure and opaque contracting constrain sovereign control over trade and resource revenues. External financiers and neighboring Senegal remain important to any modernization effort.

frictionVectors.title: Narco-trafficking and elite capture
frictionVectors.details: Transnational cocaine networks exploit limited maritime and border enforcement, reinforcing political corruption and institutional fragility. This diverts state capacity away from managing fisheries, land, and agricultural value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing Chinese financing and commercial influence around Mombasa and the Standard Gauge Railway with Western and Gulf investment. Nairobi is seeking greater local control without disrupting vital trade flows.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: External debt servicing and exposure to imported fuel constrain fiscal sovereignty. Renewable expansion improves resilience, but grid reliability and foreign capital remain strategic dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water transfers to South Africa provide essential revenue but deepen dependence on Pretoria and expose Maseru to disputes over pricing, construction delays, and project governance.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's manufacturing base relies heavily on external markets and foreign-owned supply chains. Limited fiscal capacity leaves major infrastructure decisions vulnerable to outside lenders and contractors.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and concession governance
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains central to growth but gives foreign operators substantial leverage over land, rail, and export infrastructure. The government faces pressure to improve revenue capture, transparency, and local value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Monrovia port dependence
frictionVectors.details: The port is vital to national commerce and is shaped by foreign concessionaires, shipping firms, and development partners. Liberia has limited negotiating power when balancing investment needs against strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to use production, export terminals, and budget access as leverage. Foreign commercial and political partners reinforce fragmentation by backing separate centers of influence.

frictionVectors.title: Mercenary and military footprint
frictionVectors.details: External security actors retain influence around strategic bases, borders, and energy corridors. Their presence limits unified Libyan command over territory and complicates efforts to secure sovereign resource management.

frictionVectors.title: Mining sovereignty dilemma
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, and rare-earth projects bring investment and export earnings but are largely structured around foreign capital, technology, and offtake agreements. Antananarivo is under pressure to strengthen royalties, environmental safeguards, and domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and connectivity dependence
frictionVectors.details: Weak transport links and reliance on externally financed roads, ports, and power projects give foreign partners significant agenda-setting influence. Infrastructure gaps also limit Madagascar's ability to capture more value from its resource base.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and strategic minerals
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking investment in uranium, rare earths and graphite while attempting to strengthen state oversight. Limited fiscal capacity increases reliance on foreign developers and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms constrain policy space. Foreign-exchange shortages and dependence on imported fuel expose infrastructure and food systems to external shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is pushing higher state participation and revised terms for foreign mining companies, particularly in gold. Regulatory uncertainty and permit disputes risk reducing investment while informal extraction expands.

frictionVectors.title: Security dependence and infrastructure risk
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security support has replaced much of the former Western presence but has not eliminated jihadist threats. Conflict continues to endanger transport corridors, power infrastructure and mining logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project
frictionVectors.details: Offshore gas production with Senegal and international partners offers major revenue potential but creates dependence on foreign technology, financing and export infrastructure. Border coordination and revenue-sharing remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and logistics concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and prospective green-hydrogen projects are dominated by large external investors and export corridors. This limits domestic value capture and leaves revenues vulnerable to commodity prices and geopolitical competition.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos settlement and Diego Garcia
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius has advanced its claim to the Chagos Archipelago while negotiations over the Diego Garcia base remain strategically sensitive. The issue places Port Louis between sovereignty objectives and major Indian Ocean security interests.

frictionVectors.title: External capital in ports and finance
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is balancing Indian, Chinese, Gulf and Western commercial influence around ports, logistics and financial services. Its small market makes infrastructure access and regulatory autonomy particularly vulnerable to external pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Rabat is using phosphate, fisheries, ports and renewable-energy projects in Western Sahara to consolidate territorial control and attract partners. The policy continues to generate disputes with Algeria, the Polisario Front and some European stakeholders.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dependence in strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is diversifying partnerships across Europe, the Gulf, China and the United States in ports, rail, automotive supply chains and green hydrogen. This strengthens bargaining power but creates exposure to competing external agendas.

highlights: LNG hopes return amid Cabo Delgado insecurity

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant attacks continue to threaten offshore LNG-linked logistics and constrain state access to gas-producing districts. Foreign security assistance remains important to protecting strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: LNG and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and lenders retain substantial leverage over gas development, export routes, and project timing. Mozambique faces pressure to convert LNG revenues into broader domestic industrial capacity.

highlights: Critical minerals and green hydrogen attract major capital

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of new energy assets
frictionVectors.details: International firms dominate financing and technical capacity for offshore oil, green hydrogen, and critical-mineral projects. Windfall expectations are increasing demands for local ownership, processing, and fiscal safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Logistics bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Namibia's ports, rail links, and power grid must expand rapidly to support mineral and hydrogen exports. Dependence on external infrastructure partners could limit domestic bargaining power.

highlights: Junta consolidates control over strategic resources
Export routes remain vulnerable to regional isolation

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and mining sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are renegotiating the country's relationship with foreign mining interests while seeking greater state control over uranium and other deposits. Technical, financial, and market dependence still limits how quickly that agenda can be implemented.

frictionVectors.title: Oil export corridor
frictionVectors.details: Niger's crude exports depend on long cross-border infrastructure and politically exposed transit arrangements. Regional tensions and insecurity increase the risk that production gains will not translate into reliable public revenue.

highlights: Oil-sector reform meets persistent production losses

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline theft and insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Theft, sabotage, and insecurity continue to reduce oil output and weaken the federal government's control over producing areas. International operators remain influential in financing, technology, and evacuation infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Refining and fuel sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Expanded domestic refining could reduce dependence on imported fuels, but feedstock access, regulation, and distribution remain contested. The state is balancing national-content goals against the need for foreign capital and expertise.

highlights: High state capacity meets mineral scrutiny
Regional security ties remain economically consequential

frictionVectors.title: Conflict minerals and eastern DRC
frictionVectors.details: Kigali faces sustained international scrutiny over alleged links between regional security policy, armed groups, and mineral flows from eastern DRC. Sanctions and diplomatic pressure could affect Rwanda's access to mineral markets and external finance.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic dependence on external capital
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong administrative control but relies heavily on donors, foreign investors, and regional trade corridors for infrastructure and growth. This creates exposure to shifts in Western, Gulf, and neighboring-country policy.

highlights: Balancing China, Portugal, and Western partners

frictionVectors.title: Unproven offshore hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Exploration interest has not yet translated into reliable commercial production, leaving the country dependent on external capital and technical expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-partner competition
frictionVectors.details: Portugal, China, and other partners compete for influence through infrastructure, finance, and maritime cooperation, creating leverage risks for a small state.

highlights: Gas and oil production entering statecraft

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon contract leverage
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil and gas revenues strengthen Dakar's fiscal position, but dependence on foreign operators, financing, and technology constrains control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Dakar's role as a regional logistics hub faces competition from neighboring ports and external infrastructure financiers, making concession terms and strategic autonomy sensitive issues.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure and tourism projects can expand economic capacity but leave the islands exposed to creditor influence and imported construction costs.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from cooperation with India, France, and other partners, while carefully avoiding excessive alignment amid wider Indian Ocean rivalry.

highlights: Iron ore drives renewed resource bargaining

frictionVectors.title: Mining-concession asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and other mineral projects provide revenue and jobs, but foreign ownership, export dependence, and limited domestic processing weaken Sierra Leone's control over resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining-linked rail, port, and logistics infrastructure is largely shaped by external investors, creating long-term bargaining risks over tariffs, access, and national use.

highlights: Maritime sovereignty becomes a national asset

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource competition
frictionVectors.details: Potential offshore oil and gas wealth is attracting foreign interest before Somalia has fully consolidated regulatory capacity, federal coordination, or maritime security.

frictionVectors.title: Port and security patronage
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other partners provide critical port, military, and infrastructure support, but competing agreements can fragment national authority and increase external leverage.

highlights: Power and logistics remain binding constraints

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-processing sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic beneficiation and leverage over platinum, manganese and rare-earth supply chains, while international investors resist higher regulatory and operating costs.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and port vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability, rail bottlenecks and congested ports limit sovereign control over export infrastructure and increase dependence on external capital and technical partnerships.

highlights: Oil revenues remain the fiscal lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Oil transit dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on Sudanese export infrastructure, leaving production and public finances exposed to conflict, pipeline disruption and bargaining by external operators.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-rent political economy
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and elite competition keep oil revenues concentrated, while neighboring states and foreign firms retain substantial influence over security, logistics and commercial access.

highlights: War fragments control of gold and trade routes
Red Sea access attracts competing powers

frictionVectors.title: Gold smuggling networks
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed actors and cross-border intermediaries control significant gold flows, reducing state revenue and enabling outside financing of the conflict.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, pipelines and commercial corridors is strategically contested, drawing regional and extra-regional actors into Sudan’s war economy.

highlights: Ports and LNG shape strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining power
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is using its gas potential to seek stronger state participation and domestic benefits, but financing, legal certainty and foreign consortium demands constrain policy space.

frictionVectors.title: Port-corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Dar es Salaam and other trade corridors increases Tanzania’s regional leverage while exposing infrastructure policy to Gulf, Chinese and Western commercial competition.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hinge

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé’s importance as a transshipment and land-linked trade hub brings foreign capital and strategic influence, while the state remains dependent on external operators and financing.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector control
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates remain central to resource sovereignty, but production performance, governance concerns and foreign-market exposure limit the government’s ability to capture full value.

highlights: State control tightens as fiscal pressure persists

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: European funding and cooperation remain closely tied to migration control, giving external partners influence over domestic priorities while Tunisia faces limited fiscal room.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on imported hydrocarbons and constrained investment in renewables expose Tunisia to price shocks and external financing conditions.

highlights: Oil development advances under foreign-led consortia

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sovereignty dispute
frictionVectors.details: The China-backed oil pipeline and associated fields are central to Uganda's export strategy, but financing, environmental objections, and dependence on foreign operators constrain national control.

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western actors are competing for access to Uganda's minerals and infrastructure corridors, increasing Kampala's bargaining options but also external pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: International mining firms remain dominant in extraction and processing, while Zambia is pressing for greater local beneficiation and fiscal returns amid heightened global demand for copper.

frictionVectors.title: Power shortages constrain mineral sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Electricity deficits and dependence on regional power imports threaten mining output and weaken Zambia's ability to convert mineral wealth into domestic industrial capacity.

highlights: Lithium and platinum attract intensified competition
Harare prioritizes control without broad investor trust

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals dependency
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked firms remain prominent in lithium and other mineral projects, while Zimbabwe lacks sufficient domestic processing capacity to capture the full value of its resource base.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and opaque financing
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions, governance concerns, and opaque state-linked transactions push Harare toward alternative financiers and deepen reliance on non-Western external partners.
